Shares in the company, which builds homes mainly in the north of England,plunged by 20% to a 13-year low as it predicted it would make an underlying loss of up to £10m this year, blaming weak consumer and business confidence.

“In theory, Yorkshire-based property and land developer and housebuilder Henry Boot should be a beneficiary of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s growth and levelling-up agendas, but the shares are getting flattened after a third profit warning this year,” says Russ Mould, the investment director at the platform AJ Bell.

“A weak housing market means housebuilders are cutting their purchases of land and Henry Boot, like Crest Nicholson earlier in the week, is also warning of both weak demand at its housebuilding business and the need to review the value of the land bank on its balance sheet,” Mould added.

Figures from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) show a decline in “new-build dwelling completions” in England from almost 43,000 in the second quarter of 2024 to below 36,000 in the same period this year. Annually, completions fell from about 212,000 in 2022-23 to 190,000 in 2024-25.

The weak housing market will dent the housing secretary Angela Rayner’s target of building 1.5m homes during this parliament, Most analysts believe is it is going to be about 500,000 short by the deadline in 2029.

Glenigan, a construction sector data provider, that charts the rise and fall of developments worth under £100m, says the outlook is grim after a steep decrease in the number of private-sector housing starts in the last year.

Allan Willen, the chief economist at Glenigan, says the private construction sector as a whole, including housing, infrastructure and commercial office building, has suffered over the last year.

“Build costs are high, lending has tightened and demand has softened in some sectors. As a result, numerous projects have been redesigned, delayed or cancelled.”

Those tough conditions are driving more building firms to the wall. About 3,800 firms in the construction sector went into insolvency in the last 12 months , more than any other UK industry sector.

While construction activity makes up only 6% of the economy, a decline in the wider property industry can have a devastating effect on the UK’s growth prospects. According to the latest quarterly figures, the building industry contracted by 0.7% in the three months to the end of September, holding back a rebound in the broader economy that still managed to expand by 0.7%.

Officially, the government’s 1.5m target is still in place, but a succession of profit warnings from big construction groups shows a difficult 2026 for the private sector, which is relied on for 60% of new-build home buildings, will continue next year.

The share price of Britain’s largest housebuilder, Barratt Redrow, has slumped from above 500p for much of 2024 to just 317p this week. Persimmon also suffered a drop in value after the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, followed by a slow recovery that still stops well short of values seen last year.

Reporting an annual loss of between £30m and £40m over the last year, Crest Nicholson has said this week it is struggling with a combination of costly remedial work on some sites and a slump in margins on new ones.

Meanwhile, Taylor Wimpey has cut its profit forecasts and said an industry-wide sales slowdown is in full swing and would “persist well into next year”.

Emily Williams, the director of residential research at the estate agents Savills, says a big issue facing housebuilders is a decline in prices, which she predicts will fall on average by 1.5% next year after zero growth in 2026.…

Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.

Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate set with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.

Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.

“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”

However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.

“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”

He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.

Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations .

“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”

Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online . Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.

Centrica boss memo to 400 workers at gas plant off Yorkshire coast says utility doing all it can ‘to save your jobs’

The boss of the British Gas owner Centrica has told hundreds of staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham and would do everything he could to save jobs.

Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter.

In a memo, seen by Sky News, O’Shea is understood to have expressed disappointment that the government had delayed its response to a consultation on whether to support the ageing underground gas stores over the longer term.

The Guardian understands that the government delivered its decision to Centrica in the last few weeks and the internal company memo was intended to update the facility’s staff about continuing talks.

The Rough gas storage facility supports about 400 jobs, including direct employees and contractors, but is scheduled to close at the end of March – unless the government intervenes – because it has become uneconomic to run.

Facilities typically store gas in the summer when the market price is lower, and sell it in winter when the price rises due to higher demand. But successive energy crises in recent years have upended this pattern, making it difficult to make enough money to invest in the upgrade work needed to keep the facility running.

“No decisions about roles have been made,” O’Shea wrote in the memo, according to Sky News. He reportedly added that the company was “doing everything we can to save your jobs” and that he would seek urgent talks with trade unions, Whitehall officials and the prime minister on the issue.

It is the latest in a series of warnings by Centrica over the future of the site. Centrica is listed on the FTSE 100, valued at nearly £7bn.

The jobs warning has emerged less than a fortnight after the energy company SSE told investors it would shut its Atwick gas storage site in east Yorkshire next summer unless the government offered support.

SSE said although the site continued to have “strategic importance” to the energy system as the North Sea’s domestic production declined, it was “increasingly clear” that the market would not support its continued operations.

Earlier this month, the National Energy System Operator (Neso) used a second consecutive annual report to warn that the UK was at risk of a gas supply crisis as the North Sea’s production wound down.

The report underlined concerns raised in Neso’s first annual report which found that while the UK has enough access to global gas markets to cover demand when weather is normal, if even a single piece of Britain’s ageing gas infrastructure suffered an “unlikely” outage during a very cold spell, then the UK could run out of gas.

A spokesperson for Centrica declined to comment.

Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances

Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.

The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.

Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers .

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”

He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.

However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.

In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.

It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”

The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.

Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.

Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

Workers are sad but unsurprised as closures and job losses loom, while 2,000 suppliers will take a big hit

Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future?

“I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it.

While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty.

The impact is being felt at Poundland stores across the country, as well at its head office and its distribution centres, including one in Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland last year for £1, has already collected close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures, according to documents provided to MPs. As a secured creditor on the majority of a £30m shareholder loan, Gordon Brothers is near the front of the queue to receive the proceeds of the administration including the sale of stock and store leases.

All stores currently remain open with about six main interested parties given until Sunday to put themselves in the bidding for Poundland now it is in administration. Those six potential bidders include: the Northern Irish company Martin Property Group; Zachert Private Equity, a German fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist; little-known British fund Xyra Group Holdings; and Dubai’s Premier Quality Foods.

However, many industry watchers now expect the chain to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures. Stocks are running low as the retailer is short of funds and many of its suppliers have stopped sending goods, fearing they will not be paid.

While trading had improved in recent months, it is understood that Poundland was not generating enough cash to cover its requirements and would need considerable funds to support its continued operation.

Blake, who has worked on the shop floor of one of Poundland’s Birmingham stores for 25 years, says the news has “put a downer on Christmas” but adds that he is “more worried about the future”. Now in his early 60s, he reckons it will be impossible to find another full-time contract with another retailer if his store does not remain open.

He says the administration – after Gordon Brothers rejected at least two solvent offers for the retailer and said it would not provide further funding to keep Poundland afloat – came despite a massive staff effort to turn the business around.

“The number of people coming through the doors was increasing day by day,” he said. “My store is a strong store.”

However, several other workers said that they felt the collapse of Poundland was inevitable.

“We knew at some point this was probably going to happen,” said one, who added the prospect of the store closing was “kind of worrying” but he hoped a potential buyer such as Tesco or the owner of Poundstretcher might snap up stores.

Referring to Gordon Brothers, he said: “They are doing everything legally right but not ethically right. Nobody can stop them.”

Reports this week that Poundstretcher’s US owners are lining up a sale suggest it is unlikely to rescue Poundland, though.

It is not only workers in stores that are affected. Hundreds of people work at Poundland’s two distribution centres in Bryn near Wigan and at Harlow in Essex, as well as at the head office in Walsall, near Birmingham.

Nearly 300 people are understood to work at Poundland’s eight-hectare (19-acre) site in the former coal mining village of Bryn in Ashton-in-Makerfield, within the prime minister’s constituency. It opened in 2018, and is one of the biggest retail employers in the area.

Jo Welbourne, a regional organiser for the Usdaw union, said staff are “absolutely devastated”, as many have worked at the site for a long time and live locally. “It’s devastating at any time of year but particularly around Christmas.”

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “Our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them. Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the administrators.”

The spokesperson said Poundland had “faced several years of instability” and Gordon Brothers had provided £85m in new finance “stepping in when no one else was willing to finance the business”.

Still, about 2,000 suppliers will take a considerable hit as many have supplied stock which they will not be paid for and also have further money tied up in stocks or components to make items that they expected Poundland to buy.

Davey Martens, at independent confectionery supplier Byxa, said he was owed £68,515.20 by Poundland for products already supplied. Byxa’s future would be at risk if it cannot recover “a meaningful amount” of the money owed, he added.

“This might not sound like an enormous amount,” Martens said “But for a business like ours, it is. We can’t simply absorb a loss of this size and carry on as though nothing has happened. The consequences could be devastating.

Another supplier said he was owed more than $1.2m (£915,000) for clothing items already in stores or stuck in port in the UK. He said like many other suppliers, he accepted a switch to longer payment terms of 120 days from 90 days, in the interest of helping Poundland, before Gordon Brothers said it wanted to sell the business.

The supplier is having to pay for storage in the port as Poundland does not have the funds to enable the release of the goods despite them selling well in stores.

“That is the part that is frustrating and upsetting – the small guys end up losing while big corporations make money,” he said.…

Brands know use of agents such as Meta Muse is on the rise but are unlikely to hand them the keys to the shop

Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to?

They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.

This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money.

Meta has teamed up with high street names including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys for what the Silicon Valley firm claims is a seamless, secure and time-saving tool.

“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” Meta said.

But for companies that have painstakingly transformed from bricks-and-mortar retailers into online emporiums, AI agents pose risks as well as opportunities. Will AI agents kill window shopping, ignore vast online ranges and send shoppers straight to the checkout? Will retailers be forced to discount heavily to stand out? How do they avoid being steamrollered by Silicon Valley tech titans in commercial negotiations?

John Roberts, the founder and chief executive of online electrical goods retailer AO.com, said the impact of AI agents – at present – was “relatively low” but their use as shopping assistants was clearly “a direction of travel”.

He said AO was positioning itself to get recommendations from AI agents in the same way it generally attracted customers, by offering decent prices and good service, which was winning good online reviews on sites such as Trustpilot.

“We need to work out how we are the best option for whichever AI agent you use,” Roberts said.

Working out where to invest is a challenge. Some smaller firms are almost ignoring the developing channel, waiting to see how and where it might go. However, holding back on involvement with the developing technology – such as online shopping in the early noughties – has killed off brands in the past.

Sharon Iles, a senior apparel analyst at the analytics and consultancy firm GlobalData, said those brands that have chosen to partner with Muse would get an early view of how people shop, what they bought through an AI agent and which products got recommended, which could help brands make their listings more visible.

But she said retailers “must continue to prioritise their own channels to protect what an AI agent cannot replace”.

If agents bypass retailers’ websites, said Iles, this could mean companies “miss out on the impulse items that shoppers often add while browsing”, while those selling more complex items such as apparel could find issues with the choice of fit and sizing, “which could lead to higher return rates”.

“Retailers’ own channels should remain the core of their business, and they must give consumers more reasons to shop directly,” she said.

Retailers including Sainsbury’s and Tesco have used their loyalty schemes and websites to build sizeable businesses that monetise customers’ data and sell advertising space to brands.

However, retailers cannot ignore the agents. Muse has proved successful in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

UK residents may be more cautious about agentic technology than those across the Atlantic, but the technology is entering the mainstream. This year, a third of people planning to shop during Black Friday sales intend to get help from AI – up from 19% last year, according to a recent YouGov poll.

To fans, the likes of Muse or rivals such as Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT’s Dots can be a personal secretary helping organise the boring details of life, but to others they are an untenable busybody, parsing their personal data and monetising it.

For Muse to work as Meta envisages, it not only needs access to your email, calendar and shopping apps but details of relationships on apps such as WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, your preferences and even your financial and health information.

Sainsbury’s suggests its customers can “tell Muse about their week” and the AI agent will help build a shopping list to provide for dinner parties, different dietary requirements or suggest menus and recipes.

Mark Given, the chief technology and marketing officer at the supermarket chain, said the retailer was “starting carefully, listening to customers” and using what we learn to keep making it better”.

“AI can be genuinely useful, taking on routine tasks like checking offers and building the basket, and helping customers find great value and inspiration more quickly,” he said.

In the UK, Muse must ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks the AI tool’s actions against the permissions you have granted.

Meta said Muse had no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, and it did not share users’ conversations with advertisers.

However, almost half of shoppers using AI (48%) are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations, according to YouGov. Rival research firm Kantar found only 23% trusted a chatbot’s recommendations.

Meanwhile, some retailers are territorial about which AI agents get to trawl their data. Amazon has blocked AI agents from its store, although it is reportedly in talks with Meta about allowing access. Last year, Amazon sued the AI company Perplexity over its shopping feature that automates placing orders for users.

Research from the advisory firm KPMG highlights consumer caution. It found just 12% of those planning to shop during Black Friday – a largely online sale event in the UK – intended to use an AI tool (such as prompting ChatGPT or Gemini) specifically to find deals, slightly lower than the 15% using it last year.…

Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue

R estaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.

This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.

Muse has been downloaded millions of times in the US, but it has caused chaos for restaurants. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots after restaurants on the platform were swarmed with agents that can refresh the page thousands of times and snap up all the reservations. Now, AI agents are plaguing venues in the UK.

Dave Strauss, the co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently crowned UK restaurant of the year , said he had already had an argument with a would-be diner’s AI bot.

He answers the phones in his French restaurant every day from 11am to take reservation requests and said recently he received an unnerving call: “The other day I answered the phone to an AI bot that sounded very realistic. There was something a bit wrong about it – it sounded exactly like a human being, but something was off. I asked if it was a bot and it said: ‘Yes this is an AI booking process.’”

Strauss added: “I had an argument with the AI bot and told it to never call me again. But that wasn’t very satisfying as it didn’t argue back.”

Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge, is paid by celebrities to secure a good table at top dining spots. She said she was worried about the swarm of AI bots: “I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos.”

Coke, who makes all her bookings via WhatsApp or phone calls, added: “There is now so much information you can get online about the hottest restaurants and where to go, and it is really hard to get the tables and that is why people come to me as I have personal relationships with the restaurants. With the apps, you don’t know who the client is, you have no background on who is coming in, they still might not show up. There is nothing worse for a restaurant in December when they have empty tables.”

Meta has claimed that its product can make people’s lives easier, but that has not been the case for the restaurants on the receiving end of the calls, emails and reservation app bookings.

The problem has been pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure restaurant tables are a status symbol. One of the most popular is 4 Charles Prime Rib, which serves a famous double wagyu cheeseburger, often served topped with a fried egg. It has been a popular target for AI agents, with sources at Resy saying they were having to ban multiple accounts using bots to book reservations there.

Strauss said: “There has been a constant shift to make everything as automated as possible to save a bit of money. We believe here that doesn’t work. We get a lot of emails now saying we can outsource our bookings and phone calls to AI. That makes us more keen on doing it the way that we do it. If I could get rid of online booking, I would.”

Jeremy King, who owns Simpson’s in the Strand , Arlington and the Park, said that the move towards depersonalising interactions by using AI was making him go “more analogue” in his restaurants – diners will find it much easier to snag a prime table at one of his venues by picking up the phone.

He said: “I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without.”

Such agents are likely to become more common in the UK and Meta has deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access its website instead.

The Information Commissioner’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta before Muse’s launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday the tech company had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme”, while the CMA said talks had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions fairer

Bernard Arnault’s children – described as ‘modern-day French royals’ – are subject of rivalry rumours over who will succeed him

They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest luxury goods empire, dressed in matching Dior suits – a clan so powerful they have been described as modern-day French royals.

But in recent months, the family dynasty of Bernard Arnault , 77, the billionaire head of the LVMH group whose brands range from Louis Vuitton handbags to Tiffany jewellery, has become the subject of speculation about internal rivalry over which of his children could take over the company.

This week it emerged that the health-conscious Arnault, who likes to play tennis with the Swiss champion Roger Federer, can continue to lead the family holding company until he is 95, according to a new filing, pushing back any decisions on his succession.

Last year, the age cap of Arnault’s chief executive role at LVMH was raised to 85 to allow him to stay on in the position. The fashion tycoon once joked about still leading the business at 100.

The question of which of Arnault’s five adult children could eventually lead the family company is seen as key to the French economy and the political class.

LVMH, which has more than 75 brands including fashion, perfumes and champagne, is a big employer in France.

Arnault, nicknamed the “wolf in cashmere” for his acquisitions of leading brands and whose personal wealth is estimated at more than $100bn, owns almost all of France’s business and economic press as well as the daily newspaper Le Parisien and the celebrity magazine Paris Match.

He attended Donald Trump’s second inauguration, as a personal friend, and is regularly present at official French state dinners with world leaders.

This month, Émilie Lanez published an account of what she called the emotional tensions inside the Arnault family’s unresolved succession challenge, based on what she said were hours of off-record conversations with insiders. “I was really struck by the family’s ethereal, otherworldly nature: they are like deities in a performance, and France is a spectator,” she said.

The book, Monsieur et les siens, now in discussion over a possible publication in English, traces the family’s story from Arnault’s childhood in Roubaix, in the former industrial heartland of northern France, where he took over his family’s building company before moving into property development and then luxury goods.

Lanez describes Arnault’s wife, the classical pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, working out on her treadmill in the early morning watching the HBO series Succession about a family business power-struggle, and then being at pains to publicly deny any rift or friction among the Arnault children.

The book depicts Arnault’s deep personal involvement in his children’s education. Schooling was so important in his own upbringing that when at age 10 he said farewell to his grandfather at his funeral, he put his glowing school report card into his grandfather’s clasped hands in his coffin.

When he had two children with his first wife, Anne Dewavrin, he devised a system to personally teach his daughter Delphine to read at a young age. At 51, she is now the chief executive of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most important roles at LVMH. Her brother Antoine, 49, has an important communications role, running the group’s image and environmental strategy.

Arnault later married Mercier-Arnault and had three more sons who all work for LVMH brands. Alexandre, 34, is deputy chief executive of the drinks brand Moët Hennessy; Frédéric, 32, runs the luxury fashion brand Loro Piana ; and Jean, 28, is watch director at Louis Vuitton.

When the youngest three were teenagers and preparing for higher education, Lanez writes that Arnault personally hired and interviewed tutors. The boys would come home from their day’s classes, then study with a tutor from 8pm to 11pm then go to their father’s room so he could ask them about the equations they had been tackling.

“They are likened to royals because of the power and influence they have in France,” said Lanez. “And also because they have a kind of court, courtesans and counsellors. It’s a dynasty, and the children, particularly the three youngest, have been raised to perpetuate the empire.”

Just as Arnault as a child would be shown round his father’s family building business, he regularly took his own children, and then grandchildren, on his favourite weekend activity: inspecting his luxury shops.

Arnault is aware that any family divisions can make a company vulnerable. This year, when Mercier-Arnault was promoting her latest classical music record, she did a high-profile round of media interviews in France, seeking to reassure that there were no rifts between the five children.

But with the Arnaults’ vast wealth often cited as an example of the growing power of billionaires in France amid widening economic inequality, Mercier-Arnault’s comments were scrutinised.

French media reported that in an edited radio segment she had said that being homeless could be seen as a “lifestyle choice”.

Mercier-Arnault said later on a TV show that there had been a misunderstanding and she had been referring to her experience as the carer of her late sister, a violinist who was bipolar and had died by suicide, and who had begun a relationship with a person who was homeless. She told the newspaper Libération she was “deeply sorry”.

The cast of characters in the Arnault clan includes another high-profile and influential French billionaire, the telecoms executive Xavier Niel , who is the life-partner of Delphine Arnault. The couple have two children.

“The arrival of Xavier Niel in this family was like a theatrical scenario,” Lanez said, comparing the family saga to a novel.

Asked by the Guardian to comment on the book and speculation of tension or rivalry over the succession, LVMH declined to comment.…

Residents woke up to find their vital box missing, but despite 11 months of lobbying the company now says it cannot replace it

Residents of a remote Devon village now have to drive more than a mile to send letters after their attempts to get a new postbox literally hit the rocks.

Villagers in North Huish have described a farcical near 11-month battle to challenge Royal Mail’s excuses after their box vanished without warning last January.

Royal Mail has now informed them the box will not be replaced because the ground is too stony.

The residents fear that their vanishing postbox is part of a move by Royal Mail to reduce collections.

A number of communities have complained that their postal deliveries have been cut after the regulator Ofcom relaxed Royal Mail’s performance targets last year. Ofcom is now investigating claims that parcel deliveries are being prioritised over letters after nearly a quarter of first-class mail failed to arrive on time.

The saga started in January when Royal Mail claimed that the box had been found on the ground and was beyond repair as its supporting post had rotted.

After initially agreeing to replace it after villagers’ complaints, it incorrectly claimed that the site was privately owned and it could not proceed.

Sprouts grow on a stalk, maturing from the bottom upwards. This means the largest sprouts are found at the bottom, with the smallest at the top. Supermarkets and other food retailers generally select only the mid-sized sprouts, found in the middle.

Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”.

The exchange pointed to a philosophical divide. Did the government see a tension between growth and competition? Was it worried that business investment would suffer if the competition regulator was too active?

One piece of context was the epic whine by a senior Microsoft executive about the “darkest day in our four decades in Britain” after the CMA – entirely reasonably in this column’s view at the time – gave a thumbs-down in 2023 to his company’s planned $69bn (£53bn) takeover of the video games firm Activision Blizzard.

Those events are chewed over in a punchy paper this week from two former senior Treasury officials of yesteryear, John Kingman and Shriti Vadera (the latter was also a minister in Gordon Brown’s government). Top lines: strong competition is unambiguously good for growth; we need new firms to break through and make the economy more productive. The problem is that the value of competition and disruption has become “the blind spot of current UK economic policy”, the paper says.

Fair point. Firms under five years old made 18% of all business sales in 2005; by 2021, the figure was only 10%. That decline is huge.

We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I ’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

We are encouraged to see ourselves as though we are in a race not just against other companies and even against entire countries, but also against other teams within our own company. Relationships between teams have moved from competitive to actively adversarial. The AI teams are the most siloed, the most secretive and the most separated. That’s where the race is fastest and fiercest.

People are becoming paranoid about colleagues stealing their work, reluctant to share information, secretive about the models they are developing, and worried about job security if they don’t deliver.

The natural response to these conditions is to push back against the in-house guardrails. Checks around privacy, data protection, trust and safety exist to ensure that our products don’t cause harm or break the law. But they also slow us down and restrict our work.

If a tech firm launches a new AI chatbot, the company’s trust and safety staff might consider how its users’ data is protected, or what mechanisms are needed to prevent it from encouraging self-harm or crime. They might also think about what data is being used to train the model, and where that data comes from. But those teams are increasingly being slimmed down or sidelined. And if they do raise concerns, it often doesn’t result in material changes to the final product.

In AI in particular, product-safety managers are being sidelined and the biggest companies are reducing the number of people in these roles. This depletion has been taking place gradually over the past 15 years or so, but recently it has really accelerated. It has been happening in my company and, when I look at peers in other firms, I see it there too.

This is undoubtedly resulting in more dangerous products being released. And now, the prevailing attitude within companies is that the legal teams should only worry about negative responses to our products once they are out in the world, rather than trying to consider those concerns as they are built.

The underlying belief is that our stock price will be driven up by “the next big win”, more than it will from a strategy of steady, company-wide improvements. And, even if that big win comes with legal or safety problems, the bottom line will ultimately have benefited.

At the same time, the leadership and management within tech firms has become more arrogant, with senior figures becoming more disconnected from the reality of the rest of society. This is not just the well-known CEOs but also the people a few rungs down, who are now earning salaries that mean they never have to engage with the issues most people have to face.

I still love the tech industry. But in the midst of constant restructures and redundancies, the message being sent to staff is that the biggest prize awaits as long as you compete and win. This is the culture we’re working in while handling the most powerful technologies ever developed. AI doesn’t have an ethics problem, but the people running the companies do.

He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!

Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

While many aspects of the 1990s have resurfaced – baggy jeans, Nirvana T-shirts and casual sexism – the cheque is viewed with the same disdain as dial-up internet. But I maintain that, if you must pay for something, it is truly the ideal way.

First, scribbling – holding a pen or pencil and feeling it move across the page – is enjoyable. Paying via cheque thus becomes a simple pleasure – selecting the correct ink (anything other than blue or black is frowned upon; graphite is completely unacceptable), and signing with a writing instrument rather than a finger.

Financial transactions can also be hasty – something I realised after finding myself in debt. While I now (grudgingly) have a contactless card, I still fear I might tap without checking the amount and lose a fortune. That would never happen with a cheque.

Inherent trust is required in accepting a cheque, which adds to its affability. One of my favourite pubs, The Harrow Inn in Steep, Hampshire , politely warns: “We do not take credit or debit cards. Cash and cheques are welcome.” I discovered this on a day I had neither, and the owner happily served me lunch on the understanding that a cheque would be sent in the post forthwith (it was). Even when such goodwill is manipulated, the act is described with characteristically charming language – case in point, cheques “bouncing”.

Of course, there are benefits to digital banking, some of them unexpected. A friend’s young son has a Monzo account for his pocket money. But this lady’s not for turning. I recently got a letter from HMRC informing me that I had overpaid my tax, and outlining the ways in which I might receive my refund. I don’t think I need to tell you which option I selected.

Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects , raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.

The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.

He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”

Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.

“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.

“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco , Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as gloves and masks, the investigation alleges.

Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal under UK waste export rules in almost every circumstance.

Tesco own brand slow cookers, toasters and Crockpot branded slow cookers, including at least one with a Tesco label, were found on the Accra dump.

Tesco said on Thursday it had suspended its third-party electronic waste management providers with immediate effect while it completed a full audit of them and their practices.

“We’re extremely concerned about these claims … We remain committed to removing or reducing the waste across our operations wherever we can and we work closely with experts to ensure we handle materials responsibly, in line with legal requirements and our own robust standards,” the store said.

Argos items including its own brand Cookworks products, slow cookers, toasters and food slicers were found at the dump.

Argos also said it was mounting an investigation into how the items had ended up there.

“As a responsible retailer, we have processes in place for products returned to Argos. We take these findings seriously and are reviewing the information provided to establish what further action is needed to ensure our requirements are met,” Argos said in a statement.

The investigation found dozens more British items bearing returns labels for sale, including many marked as faulty, being sold in secondhand shops in the area.

Shopkeepers said they had bought the items from brokers in the UK, who provided them as mixed shipments of home electrical equipment.

“The percentage of unusable products varies [by shipment] but sometimes it can be about 10%,” one vendor said. “What do I do with the broken ones? I put them in this box and the Agbogbloshie boys come to collect it.”

All major UK retailers who sell electrical goods operate a take-back scheme which requires them to accept and recycle disused items – for example, a shopper who brings in their old toaster when they buy a new one. The goods should be logged as e-waste and contribute to stores meeting their government-mandated recycling targets.

Under the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) regulations, the goods should be passed on to approved processors. They can only be exported if the shipper can prove they will be handled in high-quality facilities.

No facilities in west Africa are approved to receive British WEEE, according to the Environment Agency .

“Ghana is not a dumping ground for broken appliances or failed retail returns from the UK,” Joshua Awuku-Apaw, a Ghanaian environmental consultant, told Unearthed. “Shipping faulty, non-functional kitchen appliances abroad under the cover of ‘reuse’ or ‘second-hand trade’ shifts the financial, environmental, and health costs of overconsumption on to Ghanaian communities and workers … Ghana’s communities should not bear the health burden of UK retail waste.”

The investigation traced the route by which the products could have ended up in Ghana. When recently bought items are returned to shops for a refund, even when they are being returned because they are faulty, they can enter a separate stream, the liquidation market, along with other consumer returns, the investigation found.

“Just because somebody in the supermarket says it’s not working, doesn’t always mean they’ve technically declared it as waste,” said e-waste expert Mark Sayers.

Many of the items Greenpeace found in Agbogbloshie and second-hand stores had stickers labelling the goods as “untested return”.

The investigation alleged that returned goods are often sold off in bulk, at a fraction of their shop shelf-price. Sometimes this takes place via the retailers’ own stock liquidation channels where pallets of returns, including job lots of small household electricals, are sold.

The lots are bought by “jobbers” – individuals and small businesses who buy the goods by the palletload and set about extracting any value they can – whether by listing items individually on eBay or Vinted, selling them in bargain-bin stores or exporting them.

Jim Puckett, founder of Basel Action Network, which campaigns against the export of e-waste to poorer countries, said that treating untested returns as anything other than waste was a “major loophole”.

“It should be considered waste until proven otherwise,” he said. “Especially if people are buying it at auction or whatever and shipping it all around the world.”

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Illegal waste exports are a serious crime. There is no excuse for exporting waste to be dumped or landfilled overseas. Waste leaving England must be sent for legitimate recovery or recycling.

“New controls mean exports of waste electrical and electronic equipment must be notified and approved before they leave the country. The Environment Agency is using intelligence to intervene earlier, target suspicious shipments and disrupt the criminals behind illegal waste exports.”

“Anyone who breaks the law risks having shipments stopped, facing prosecution and financial penalties. Waste criminals should be in no doubt, we are watching, we are acting and you will face the consequences.”…

It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

I n the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today.

It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure, and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai.

After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation.

The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition.

Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical.

Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals.

Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United . On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liverpool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s Premier League history.

“Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.

That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that quickly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool , under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.

De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

Pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

Liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

The first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.

Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from his fellow £100m+ recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.

Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

Manchester United lose 4-0 to Liverpool after early red

Argentinian suffers club’s joint-heaviest debut defeat

Mauricio Pochettino argued that Leny Yoro was wrongly sent off and that Manchester United were earlier denied a penalty against Liverpool after suffering the joint-heaviest debut defeat in the club’s history.

Liverpool’s emphatic 4-0 win ensured Pochettino equalled Lal Hilditch’s unwanted record from 1926 of losing his first United game by such a scoreline. United’s 34 goals conceded across all competitions this season are the most by any team in European football’s top five leagues.

United were reduced to 10 men after only eight minutes when Yoro was shown a straight red card for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. “He was clearly the last man and it was clearly a foul,” said the Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola.

“It is painful for me and for them but we played for more than 80 minutes at Anfield with 10 men. You can be critical of the team, but it’s a penalty for Mbeumo. We can make a mistake and we were punished. They can make a mistake and they were not punished.”

Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino .

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.

Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick .

Eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.

Very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.

The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.

Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.

Yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.

“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.

Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.

By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s new project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.

After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.

Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.

In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.

Going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.

It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.

Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.

They were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.

A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.

This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.

Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.

De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

“I ’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.

Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille , wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”

This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”

Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”

Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”

The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”

Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”

That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”

Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”

This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”

Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.

There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”

Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”

Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux , the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”…

Rivals engage law firm Wiggin as they seek damages

Claim could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds

Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham are using the same law firm to prepare a legal claim against Manchester City for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds.

The clubs have engaged the services of the London-based media, entertainment and technology specialists Wiggin. Arsenal are using their retained lawyers, HFS Kramer, to prepare their own claim.

A source with knowledge of the case disclosed there had been a degree of cooperation between the clubs using Wiggin, because they have also engaged the same analysts to assess the size of the potential losses allegedly caused by City’s financial cheating , but that they would bring separate claims for damages.

“The cases are similar but different,” the source said. “The ultimate causation may be the same, but the damages will be different so they will be separate claims.”

Another source disclosed that Tottenham initially engaged Wiggin while Daniel Levy was the chair and were the first club to make legal moves against City after they were charged with financial fair play breaches in February 2023, with United and Liverpool following their lead.

Those three clubs and Arsenal lodged legal notices in November 2024 reserving their right to seek compensation against City to avoid their potential claims being ruled time-barred, one of the mechanisms through which City succeeded in 2020 in having a two-year ban from the Champions League imposed by Uefa for similar alleged offences lifted by the court of arbitration for sport.

Standard breach of contract claims have a six-year statute limitation from the moment they are made public, and with the allegations of City’s rule-breaking first published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in November 2018, four of the other members of the big six acted to reserve their rights.

Chelsea did not instruct lawyers to begin a claim against City at that point, and are not believed to have done so since, despite the fact that extensions to the time limit can be granted in cases of fraud and concealment.

The four clubs who are preparing legal action have stepped up their activities since the Premier League announced in September that City had been found guilty of the vast majority of more than 100 charges against them, with an independent commission ruling that the club had artificially inflated its income by more than £900m through the use of “sham contracts” between 2009 and 2018.

Tottenham are likely to make the biggest claim against City because they missed out on Champions League qualification to them on four occasions during that period, with dropping into the Europa League costing them more than £120m.

United and Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to City during years when City have been found to have inflated their income, in 2012 and 2014 respectively, costing them prize money and commercial revenue and bonuses.

Arsenal missed out on Champions League qualification by finishing fifth in the Premier League in 2017, the start of a six-season run outside Europe’s elite competition that combined will have cost them hundreds of millions of pounds, as City ended up third.

Arsenal also sold five key players to City during the period of their breaches – Kolo Touré, Gaël Clichy, Emmanuel Adebayor, Bacary Sagna and Samir Nasri – and may claim additional losses on the grounds that their purchases were artificially funded.

Everton, Newcastle and Chelsea also missed out on Champions League places during the relevant period, and numerous clubs including Hull were relegated in part owing to their results against City.

Stoke lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, costing them a Europa League place, and their then manager, Tony Pulis, said in October that the club should be awarded the trophy.

City have denied wrongdoing since being charged almost four years ago and have launched an appeal against the independent commission’s verdict , which will be heard by a new three-person panel next month. After launching their appeal in October, City issued a statement saying the commission’s judgment contained “multiple clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe” and that “the club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all its positions, relating to this case”.

Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January

The new cap, set by the regulator Ofgem , works out at £2,166 for a typical annual gas and electricity bill – up £443 on the October to December equivalent. Yet, even though there are dozens of deals available to fix for less, two-thirds of households remain on the default tariff that tracks the cap.

So what is stopping people from switching? We asked for people’s views on why they plan to change provider or stick with a variable account.

For Andy, a big concern is locking in at the top of the market. He has switched numerous times to save money but with variable tracker rates “eye-wateringly high”, he says he worries “that if I fix now at an increased rate, prices could start to come down”.
